definition: An AI system that plans and carries out multi-step tasks with tools, under supervision. For example: read an order, check capacity, propose a slot, flag the risk and draft the supplier email.
A confident but wrong answer from a model. It is a property of the technology, not a bug the next model will fix: grounding in company data reduces it, and human review controls it.
A model that spends extra computation working through a problem before answering. It does better on multi-step problems but is slower and costs more per answer.
Everything a model can consider in one call: instructions, documents and conversation. What is in neither its training nor its context does not exist for the model.
Changing a model's weights by training it further on examples. It shapes behavior, format and style, but it is rarely the first step for a company and is a poor way to add changing knowledge.
Using a trained model to produce an answer. It is paid per token, on every call, so it is the running cost of any AI application.
The instructions and context given to a model in a call. Better context beats clever wording: what the model needs to know must be put in front of it.

A method that fetches relevant documents and puts them in the model's context, grounding answers in company data without changing the model. Typical failures: wrong passages retrieved, missing or stale documents.
A chunk of text, about three quarters of an English word on average. Prices, speed and limits are counted in tokens. Non-English text, numbers and codes often take more tokens.
Building a model by learning from very large datasets. It is done by labs, is expensive and happens rarely. A model does not learn from your conversations by default.
A list of numbers (a vector) that captures the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning get similar vectors, which makes semantic search possible.
A set of real cases with expected outputs, run before and after every change to a prompt, model or pipeline. Without evals, quality is an opinion.
An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources. A connection is built once and can then be used by many AI clients.
Search that finds text with similar meaning, not identical words, by comparing embeddings. It does not match exact codes reliably, such as part numbers or order numbers.
Model output that follows a defined format, such as JSON matching a schema, so software can use it directly. It should still be validated before use.
A setting that controls how much a model's output varies. A low temperature reduces variation but does not guarantee identical outputs for the same input.
The model emits a structured request to call a tool; the application decides whether to execute it and returns the result. This is how agents act on systems, and where permissions live.
The mechanism that lets each token weigh every other token in the context. Its naive cost grows quadratically with context length, and recall across long contexts is uneven.
Whether an answer is actually supported by the documents or data the model was given. Groundedness checks catch answers that sound right but are not backed by what was retrieved.
Retrieval that combines keyword search with vector search. It is needed for exact identifiers such as part numbers, SKUs, machine ids and order numbers, which embeddings alone miss.
The raw scores a model outputs over its vocabulary for the next token. They are turned into probabilities, and sampling settings such as temperature then pick the token.
Reusing the processing of a repeated prompt prefix, such as fixed instructions or a long document, across calls. It cuts both cost and latency.
A second step in retrieval that reorders the candidate passages by relevance to the question before they reach the model. It raises the precision of what the model is given.
An ontology filled with a company's actual facts, stored as nodes and relationships. It lets a model answer questions that span several linked facts, such as suppliers, machines and defective lots.
A formal, machine-readable model of the business: what exists, how things relate, which rules apply and which actions are allowed. The model is rented; the ontology is the company's own asset.
A hierarchy of categories, such as product families and subfamilies. It is not an ontology: it classifies things but does not state their relationships, rules or allowed actions.
A type carries shared capabilities and constraints, such as rates, allowed product families and setup rules for a machine type. An instance is one real thing, such as machine #7, with today's state.
Mapping the same supplier, material or machine when it appears under different codes across systems. Without explicit mapping, the same thing is counted or treated as several.
A real decision rule that lives in spreadsheets and experts' heads rather than in any system. Extract it by walking recent real cases, asking for exceptions and studying overrides.
Enterprise resource planning: the core business system for orders, inventory and finance. It stays as the system of record; its master data, such as rates and lead times, is often wrong.
The system that officially owns a piece of data; every other source is a copy. Keep the ERP as the system of record and add a thin layer of agents and apps on top.
Advanced planning and scheduling: a system that builds production plans and schedules against capacity and constraints, between the ERP and the shop floor.
Computerized maintenance management system: the system that plans and records maintenance work, breakdowns and spare parts for equipment.
Manufacturing execution system: the plant system that runs and records shop-floor execution, such as which order runs on which machine, when, and with what result.
The documented process and how work actually happens diverge. Data produced by the official process can mislead, so watch the real work before modeling or automating it.
Product lifecycle management: the system that holds product data, such as designs, specifications, bills of materials and their revisions.
Quality management system: the system that holds quality data and processes, such as inspections, nonconformities, corrective actions and lot release.
Supervisory control and data acquisition: systems that monitor and control machines and collect their signals, usually stored over time in historians.
Warehouse management system: the system that manages stock locations, receipts, picking and shipments inside a warehouse.
An inventory of the data a use case needs across three layers: system data, spreadsheet data and data in people's heads. Much of what agents need lives outside any system of record.
A data pipeline that gives the same result however many times it runs on the same input. It relies on stable business keys, upserts, incremental loads and checks at each stage.
A standard model of plant system levels: 0 to 2 for sensing and control, 3 for manufacturing operations such as the MES, and 4 for business planning such as the ERP.
Turning capacity freed by software into money through decisions, such as filling freed hours with orders or stopping overtime. It needs a client-side owner with a mandate and authority.
A gain that the client's finance team has signed: measurable, attributable and backed by the CFO. Until then it does not count, however good the project team's model looks.
The agreed reference a gain is measured against: 12 rolling months when there is seasonality, never fewer than 6, on a frozen, named perimeter. Co-build it with finance before any software runs.
Revenue minus variable costs. Freed capacity is valued at contribution margin only when the extra output can be sold, capped by the order backlog; otherwise at avoided variable cost.
The one-time cost of getting a gain, such as software, people and change. Gains are stated gross or net of it, and payback is this cost divided by the monthly net run-rate.
Adjusting the baseline for changes in volume, mix and price, so a gain reflects the improvement and not a busier or quieter period. For example: baseline rate × actual volume, per product family.
The recurring level a gain reaches once fully in place, usually expressed per month or year. It must be distinguished from what has actually been realized so far.
Building a gain figure a second, independent way, such as top-down from the P&L and bottom-up from hours × rates. Within 20 to 30%, present it; beyond, find the error.
The cash tied up in running the business: inventory plus receivables minus payables. Releasing it is counted once as cash, and recurring only as the carrying cost saved.
An engineer who embeds in the client's operation and owns a business outcome in production: production code, running systems, measured euro gains. Not a consultant, a pre-sales engineer or staffing.
The first site where a deployment proves itself, with gains reconciled to the P&L, before it extends to other sites. Pilot sites are rarely representative, so check before generalizing.
An internal operational person with a formal role, legitimacy and a direct line to the software teams, who carries the tools after the project team leaves.
The path people go through when their work changes: denial, resistance, exploration, commitment. Performance dips before it rises, so plan for the dip.
The step that limits the output of the whole system. An hour lost there is lost for the whole system; an hour saved elsewhere is a mirage.
Overall equipment effectiveness: availability × performance × quality. It shows how much of a machine's planned time produces good parts at the expected rate.
Switching a machine or line from one product to another, during which it does not produce good parts. Sequencing by product family and SMED methods reduce changeover time.
A reinforcing loop: expedites break sequences, causing more changeovers, less capacity, more lateness and more expedites. Break it at the cheapest link rather than expediting better.
Work in progress = throughput × lead time, so lead time = work in progress ÷ throughput. Releasing more work into a full shop makes orders later, not earlier.
On time in full: the share of orders delivered on the promised date and in the full quantity. It is stricter than on-time delivery (OTD) alone.
The pace of production needed to meet customer demand: available time divided by demand. It differs from cycle time (time to complete one unit) and lead time (time through the whole flow).
A method to improve flow: identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it only after exploiting it, and repeat, because the constraint moves.
Orders or material that have started but are not finished. With throughput fixed by the bottleneck, more WIP means longer lead times, not more output.
A design where AI proposes and an accountable person approves consequential or irreversible actions. Controls match the cost of error; approving every output is not the safest design.

An attack where instructions hidden in input, directly or through documents, emails or web pages, hijack a model. Defend with least privilege, separate reads and writes, and human approval for writes.
